cls: Endogenous purine nucleoside - antiarrhythmic (Vaughan-Williams unclassified / Class V)
quick: 6 mg rapid IV push; if no response in 1-2 min, 12 mg, may repeat 12 mg once
Not applicable - IV use in monitored/emergency setting
Limited data; used in pregnancy for maternal SVT when needed
Very short half-life (<10 s); not expected to be detectable in milk
No dose adjustment needed (metabolised in blood/tissues, not renally)
No dose adjustment needed (not hepatically eliminated)
Not relevant to acute single-dose IV emergency use
Continuous ECG and blood pressure; have resuscitation equipment ready
summary: Adenosine is an endogenous purine nucleoside given as a rapid IV bolus to terminate paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT), including AV-nodal re-entry and accessory-pathway (WPW) circuits, by transiently blocking AV-nodal conduction. Its extremely short half-life (under 10 seconds) means effects - including a brief period of asystole and flushing - resolve within seconds. It must be given as a fast push immediately followed by a saline flush, with continuous ECG monitoring.
indications: Conversion to sinus rhythm of paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (PSVT), including PSVT associated with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome
Diagnostic aid: pharmacologic stress in myocardial perfusion imaging (adenosine stress test)
Diagnostic unmasking of underlying atrial activity in wide/narrow complex tachycardia

dosage.d: 6 mg rapid IV bolus over 1-2 seconds
dosage.n: Follow immediately with rapid saline flush; via peripheral line as close to patient as possible

dosage.d: 12 mg rapid IV bolus if no response within 1-2 minutes
12 mg rapid IV bolus if still no response
dosage.n: Doses above 12 mg are not recommended

dosage.d: Same as adult: 6 mg then 12 mg, 12 mg
0.05-0.1 mg/kg rapid bolus, increasing by 0.05-0.1 mg/kg every 1-2 min
dosage.n: Up to maximum single dose 0.3 mg/kg (not exceeding 12 mg)

admin: For rapid IV bolus use ONLY - give over 1-2 seconds
Administer directly into a vein or into the IV line as close to the patient as possible
Follow each dose immediately with a rapid saline flush
Use only on continuous ECG monitoring with resuscitation facilities available
Do not refrigerate (crystallisation may occur); solution must be clear
moa: Adenosine acts on A1 receptors in the AV node, activating inward-rectifier potassium currents and inhibiting calcium influx. This slows conduction through the AV node, interrupting re-entry circuits that involve the AV node and restoring normal sinus rhythm. Its diagnostic vasodilatory effect (coronary stress imaging) is mediated by A2A receptors on vascular smooth muscle.

absolute: Second- or third-degree AV block (except with functioning pacemaker)
Sinus node disease such as sick sinus syndrome or symptomatic bradycardia (except with functioning pacemaker)
relative: Asthma or bronchospastic lung disease (may provoke bronchospasm)
Recent myocardial infarction or unstable angina
Concurrent dipyridamole (markedly potentiates) or carbamazepine (increases heart block)

preg: Limited human data. Adenosine has been used to terminate maternal SVT during pregnancy when clinically required; its extremely short half-life limits fetal exposure. Use when the benefit justifies potential risk.
lact: No data on milk excretion, but the ultra-short half-life (under 10 seconds) makes meaningful infant exposure from a single therapeutic dose implausible. Considered compatible.
renal: No dose adjustment required. Adenosine is rapidly taken up by cells and metabolised in the blood and tissues, independent of renal function.
hepatic: No dose adjustment required. Elimination does not depend on hepatic metabolism.

major: Dipyridamole (blocks adenosine uptake - greatly potentiates effect; reduce adenosine dose or avoid)
Methylxanthines (theophylline, caffeine) antagonise adenosine - larger doses may be needed
moderate: Digoxin and verapamil (rare reports of ventricular fibrillation in combination)
interactions.food: Caffeine and other methylxanthines reduce effectiveness; withhold caffeine before adenosine stress testing
interactions.alcohol: No clinically significant interaction relevant to acute single-dose use
interactions.diagnostics: Used as a diagnostic agent itself; transient AV block can unmask underlying atrial flutter/fibrillation on ECG

common: Transient sinus bradycardia or brief asystole
serious: Prolonged asystole or high-grade AV block
Atrial fibrillation (including in WPW, rarely with rapid ventricular response)
rare: Ventricular arrhythmias including torsades / ventricular fibrillation
emergency: Sustained asystole or symptomatic high-grade AV block

monitoring: Continuous ECG during and after administration
Heart rate and rhythm during the transient AV-block phase
counsel: This medicine is given by a doctor in a monitored setting
You may briefly feel flushing, chest tightness, or shortness of breath - these pass within seconds
Tell staff if you have asthma or any breathing problems
Avoid caffeine before a planned adenosine stress test
pk: Less than 10 seconds (rapidly metabolised in blood and tissues)
Very brief - effect resolves within seconds to under a minute
Store at room temperature 15-30 C; do NOT refrigerate (may crystallise); discard unused portion
pearls: Warn the patient of an unpleasant but very brief sense of impending doom/chest pressure before giving
Always follow the bolus with a rapid saline flush - inadequate delivery is the commonest cause of failure
Transient asystole of a few seconds is expected; ensure resuscitation equipment is at hand
Reduce the dose substantially in patients on dipyridamole and increase (or use alternative) in those on theophylline/heavy caffeine
Does not convert atrial flutter or fibrillation but may transiently slow the rate to reveal underlying rhythm
missed: Not applicable - adenosine is a single-use acute emergency or diagnostic agent given by a clinician, not a scheduled self-administered drug.
overdose: The ultra-short half-life makes sustained overdose effects unlikely; if prolonged high-grade AV block or asystole occurs it is usually self-limiting within seconds. Methylxanthines such as aminophylline (a competitive antagonist) may be used if effects persist. Provide supportive care and continuous cardiac monitoring.
